content: 1. Two filtration units are operating in parallel to ensure effective water treatment. 2. Disinfection is achieved through chlorination to inactivate or kill microorganisms present in the water. 3. Treated water is stored in four interconnected tanks located on-site at the water treatment facility. 4. The distribution system includes household piped water supply and public taps for accessibility. 5. At the household level, bulk water storage, additional water treatment (such as filtration or boiling), and post-treatment storage are implemented to ensure water safety. Key water quality challenges include: 6. Seasonal variations in source water quality, with high turbidity observed during the wet season. 7. Runoff from human settlements, agricultural activities, and light industries upstream of the raw water intake point, which can introduce contaminants. 8. Intermittent water supply due to limited capacity of the water treatment plant. 9. Unaccounted water losses caused by leakages and illegal connections, which may compromise water quality and system efficiency. Operational Monitoring Plan Development: 10. Sample points for water quality testing were strategically selected based on existing control measures within the water supply system. 11. Twelve sample points were identified in the distribution system, representing the start, middle, and end of the system. 12. In Bajo town, the largest population center in the Wangdue water supply system, four sample points were selected to ensure comprehensive monitoring. 13. The sampling schedule was designed to collect one sample from Bajo town each week, with all 12 sample points tested within a one-month period. 14. Vulnerable populations, including schools and hospitals, were also represented in the sampling plan. Water Quality Testing and Corrective Actions: 15. Turbidity is monitored at the sedimentation tank inlet using a turbidity meter, with monthly testing (weekly during the monsoon season). 16. If critical limits are exceeded, corrective actions include adjusting chlorine dosage, ensuring optimal operation of chlorine pumps, and verifying proper preparation of chlorine batches according to standard operating procedures (SOPs). 17. Additional water quality tests may be conducted to assess the extent of the problem, and flushing of water mains may be required if the issue is localized. Glossary of Key Terms: 18. Abstraction refers to the process of harvesting raw water for drinking-water supply. 19. Aesthetic qualities of drinking water relate to its taste, odor, or appearance. 20. Backflow is the unintentional reverse flow of contaminated water into the drinking-water system. 21. Chlorine decay describes the reduction in chlorine concentration as water moves through the supply system due to reactions with organic and inorganic materials. 22. Chlorine demand is the extent of reaction between chlorine and materials in water that consume chlorine, reducing its concentration. 23. Chlorine disinfection involves adding chlorine to drinking water to inactivate or kill microorganisms. 24. Coagulation is a water treatment process where a coagulant is added to assist in removing organic and inorganic materials. 25. Contact time is the time required for chlorine to effectively disinfect drinking water. 26. Control measure refers to actions within a water supply system to prevent or eliminate hazards or reduce them to acceptable levels. 27. Corrective actions are timely measures taken to restore effective operation of a control measure when critical limits are exceeded. 28. Critical limit is the threshold at which a control measure is no longer effective, posing a potential water quality risk. 29. Cross connections are unintended connections between drinking-water pipes and non-drinking-water pipes, such as sewage or recycled water pipes. 30. Illegal connections are unauthorized connections to the drinking-water supply, often causing leakages and introducing risks like backflow or cross connections. 31. Intermediate storage refers to treated drinking-water storage after treatment, such as in reservoirs or tanks. 32. Jar test is a laboratory test to determine the optimal coagulant dose by adding different concentrations of coagulant to water samples at varying pH levels. 33. Operational monitoring involves routine water quality checks to ensure the water supply system operates within acceptable limits and control measures are effective. 34. Residual chlorine is the concentration of chlorine remaining in drinking water after disinfection, protecting it from recontamination during distribution. 35. Riparian buffer zone is a vegetated area adjacent to a water source that acts as a buffer, trapping particles and reducing water quality impacts. 36. Secondary chlorination is the addition of chlorine within the distribution system to maintain residual chlorine levels. 37. Source water refers to raw water used for drinking-water supplies, including groundwater, rainwater, and surface water sources. 38. Turbidity is the cloudy appearance of water caused by organic and inorganic particles. 39. Water Safety Plan is a comprehensive approach to drinking-water quality risk assessment and management, from the catchment to the consumer. WHO/DFAT Partnership for Water Quality and Health: 40. The WHO/AusAID (DFAT) partnership has been promoting water safety plans (WSPs) in South-East Asia for over a decade. 41. WSPs aim to improve water quality throughout supply systems, benefiting all users by enhancing health and system sustainability. 42. One major challenge for sustainable WSP implementation, especially in smaller systems, is effective operational monitoring to ensure control measures remain functional. 43. WHO engaged an operational water quality expert to assist Bhutan and Timor-Leste in improving their monitoring practices through tailored training programs and implementation of SOPs for water quality monitoring instrumentation. 44. These SOPs are now published to meet the growing demand for training materials and manuals in this technical area.
